title: The Greatest Man of the East
subtitle: Job 1:1–21
description: A blameless man loses everything in one day, and blesses God anyway.
paragraphs: The book opens with a sentence that tells you almost nothing you can date: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job.” No king is named, no year is given, and Uz is never located. What the book says about the man himself is total: he was “blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil.” Everything that follows happens to a man the text has already cleared of charges, and the story will need you to remember that.

Job was rich in the currency of his world. He had seven sons and three daughters, and he owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 female donkeys, and a very large number of servants, which made him the greatest man of all the people of the East. His sons took turns holding feasts in their homes and invited their sisters to eat and drink with them, and when the feasting days were over, Job would send for his children to purify them, rising early to offer burnt offerings for all of them. “Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts,” he thought. This was his regular practice, a father covering sins nobody knew about.

Then the story steps behind a curtain Job never sees behind. One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came with them, fresh, he said, “From roaming through the earth,” and walking back and forth in it. God Himself raised the subject: “Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil.” Satan's answer questioned the arrangement, not the man: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” God had placed a hedge around him, blessed his work, and multiplied his possessions. “But stretch out Your hand and strike all that he has, and he will surely curse You to Your face.” The permission came with a border: “Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself.”

The blow fell in a single day, while Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house. A messenger came: the Sabeans had taken the oxen and donkeys and put the servants to the sword. While he was still speaking, another: the fire of God had fallen and consumed the sheep and the servants. While he was still speaking, another: Chaldean raiding bands had taken the camels. Each man ended with the same words: “I alone have escaped to tell you!” Then the last messenger: a mighty wind from the desert struck the four corners of the house, and it collapsed on the young people, and they were dead.

Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. Then he fell to the ground and worshiped, and what he said is the first famous line of the book: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD.” The narrator closes the chapter with a verdict the rest of the book will lean on: “In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing.”

title: Skin for Skin
subtitle: Job 2:1–13
description: The attack reaches Job's own body, his wife urges him to curse God, and three friends come to sit with him.
paragraphs: The council met again. The sons of God presented themselves before the LORD, Satan came with them, and God raised the same subject with an addition: “He still retains his integrity, even though you incited Me against him to ruin him without cause.” Job had lost everything countable in one day and had blessed the name of the LORD anyway. The accusation adjusted its aim.

“Skin for skin!” Satan replied. “A man will give up all he owns in exchange for his life.” Possessions were one thing, the argument ran; a man's own flesh was another. “But stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones, and he will surely curse You to Your face.” The permission again came with a border: “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life.” So Satan went out and infected Job with terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head. Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself, and he sat among the ashes.

That is where the only member of his household left to him spoke. Job's wife said, “Do you still retain your integrity? Curse God and die!” His answer was a rebuke and a question: “You speak as a foolish woman speaks,” he told her. “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” The narrator repeats his clearance a second time: in all this, Job did not sin in what he said. Whatever the argument had predicted, Job's mouth had still not cursed God.

Word of the disaster had traveled. Job's three friends, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, heard about all the adversity that had come upon him, and they made an appointment together to go and sympathize with him and comfort him. When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, they could barely recognize him. They wept aloud, tore their robes, and threw dust in the air over their heads.

Then the three men did the best thing anyone does in the whole book's long argument, and they did it before anyone argued anything. They sat on the ground with Job for seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, because they saw how intense his suffering was. The silence lasted a week. What broke it was not the comforters. It was Job.

title: May the Day of My Birth Perish
subtitle: Job 3:1–26
description: After seven silent days, Job opens his mouth and curses the day he was born.
paragraphs: After seven days of silence, Job opened his mouth, and what came out startled everyone who thought they knew what he would say. He did not curse God. He cursed the day he was born. “May the day of my birth perish, and the night it was said, ‘A boy is conceived.’” He called down darkness on the calendar itself: let that day be reclaimed by gloom, let no light shine on it, let it not appear among the days of the year. He wished the night had shut the doors of the womb and hidden all this sorrow from his eyes.

“Why did I not perish at birth; why did I not die as I came from the womb?” Why were there knees to receive him and breasts to nurse him? Had he died at birth, he argued, he would now be lying down in peace, asleep and at rest, in the one country where rank means nothing, “with kings and counselors of the earth, who built for themselves cities now in ruins,” or with princes who had gold. Or if he had been hidden like a stillborn child, he would never have seen daylight at all.

Death, in Job's speech, is the great leveler, and he describes it almost with longing. “There the wicked cease from raging, and there the weary find rest.” The captives enjoy their ease there and no longer hear the oppressor's voice. “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.” It is the first sign of where his mind is going: not toward accusation yet, but toward sleep, toward an end of being hunted by pain.

Then the questions turn from the grave to the living. “Why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter of soul,” to men who long for death and it does not come, who search for it like hidden treasure and would rejoice at reaching the grave? Why is life given “to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?” The hedge Satan once mocked as protection has become, in Job's mouth, a wall with him trapped inside it.

He closed with the plain facts of his days. Sighing came when food was set before him, and his groans poured out like water. “For the thing I feared has overtaken me, and what I dreaded has befallen me.” The man who once rose early to offer sacrifices against sins nobody had committed had feared something all along, and it had arrived. “I am not at ease or quiet; I have no rest, for trouble has come.” The silence of the seven days was over. The argument was about to begin.

title: Eliphaz and the Night Vision
subtitle: Job 4:1–5:27
description: Eliphaz answers with a night vision and an old doctrine: the innocent do not perish.
paragraphs: Eliphaz the Temanite answered first, and he began like a friend. “If one ventures a word with you, will you be wearied? Yet who can keep from speaking?” He reminded Job of his own record: Job had instructed many, strengthened feeble hands, steadied those who stumbled. Now trouble had come to Job himself, and he was dismayed. “Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope?” Then, gently, he laid down the doctrine the whole debate would run on: “Consider now, I plead: Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” As he had observed, “those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble reap the same.”

To back the doctrine, Eliphaz told of a night visitation. A word had come to him secretly, in disquieting visions, when deep sleep falls on men. Fear made his bones shudder, and a spirit glided past his face so that the hair on his body bristled. It stood still, a form he could not make out, and he heard a whispering voice: “Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?” If God puts no trust in His own servants and charges His angels with error, how much more men, who dwell in houses of clay, crushed like a moth, smashed from dawn to dusk. It was a true-sounding speech about human frailty. Eliphaz was applying it to a man whose losses he had watched for seven silent days.

From the vision he turned to observation. He had seen a fool taking root, and suddenly the man's house was cursed; his sons were far from safety, crushed without a defender. Distress does not spring from the dust, he said, and trouble does not sprout from the ground. “Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward.” The remedy was not complaint. If Eliphaz were Job, he would appeal to God and lay his cause before Him, the One who does “great and unsearchable things, wonders without number,” who gives rain to the earth, sets the lowly on high, and thwarts the schemes of the crafty so that injustice shuts its mouth.

Then came the offer, stated as blessing. “Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.” “For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.” Eliphaz promised rescue from six calamities and no harm in seven, laughter at destruction and famine, a secure tent, offspring like the grass of the earth, and a grave reached in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.

He ended with the confidence of a man presenting research: “Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself.” The logic was clean, old, and orderly. Suffering of this size must have a cause on Job's side of the ledger, discipline would end it, and repentance was the door. Everything Eliphaz said assumed one thing he never examined: that he already knew why this had happened.

title: The Arrows of the Almighty
subtitle: Job 6:1–7:21
description: Job calls his friends faithless streams and asks God why He will not pardon him.
paragraphs: Job's answer began with the weight of it. If only his grief could be weighed and placed with his calamity on the scales, it would outweigh the sand of the seas; no wonder his words had been rash. “For the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me; my spirit drinks in their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.” Does a wild donkey bray over fresh grass, he asked, or an ox low over its fodder? Creatures cry out over what is wrong, not over nothing.

His request of God was not restoration. It was an end. If only God would grant it: “that God would be willing to crush me, to unleash His hand and cut me off!” Even in that request he held one comfort and one joy through unrelenting pain: “that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.” What strength did he have, that he should still hope? Was his flesh made of bronze? A despairing man, he said, should have the kindness of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.

Instead, his friends had become desert streams. He called his brothers “as faithless as wadis,” seasonal watercourses that swell with melting snow and vanish in the heat exactly when travelers need them. The caravans of Tema look for water and arrive confounded and disappointed. “For now you are of no help; you see terror, and you are afraid.” He had never begged them for a bribe or asked them to deliver him from an enemy. What he asked was instruction: “Teach me, and I will be silent. Help me understand how I have erred.” “How painful are honest words! But what does your argument prove?” And then, turning the challenge around: “Would I lie to your face?” “Reconsider; do not be unjust. Reconsider, for my righteousness is at stake.”

Chapter 7 widens from the friends to God Himself. A man's days are like a hired hand's, Job said, and his own allotment was months of futility and nights of misery. His flesh was clothed with worms and encrusted with dirt; his skin cracked and festered. His days were swifter than a weaver's shuttle and ended without hope. “Remember that my life is but a breath. My eyes will never again see happiness.”

Near the end he addressed the watcher directly. “What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him,” that You attend to him every morning and test him every moment? “Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity?” Soon he would lie in the dust, and God would seek him, but he would be no more. The debate had begun as comfort. Within two speeches it had become something else: a suffering man, convinced of his innocence, demanding to know what charge stood against him, and friends determined to explain a heaven they had not seen.

title: Bildad, and God's Unsearchable Greatness
subtitle: Job 8:1–9:35
description: Bildad explains the children's deaths, and Job asks for a mediator who does not exist.
paragraphs: Bildad the Shuhite answered with less patience than Eliphaz. “How long will you go on saying such things? The words of your mouth are a blustering wind.” Then he put the doctrine as a question about God's character: “Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right?” And he applied it to the worst of Job's losses directly. “When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion.” They were Job's ten children, buried in one afternoon, explained in one sentence by a man who had not been there when the wind came.

Bildad's counsel was the same door Eliphaz had pointed to, held open. If Job would earnestly seek God and ask for mercy, if he was pure and upright, God would even now rouse Himself on his behalf and restore his righteous estate. Though his beginnings were modest, his latter days would flourish. For authority he appealed backward: inquire of past generations and consider the discoveries of their fathers, “For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow.” The fathers, he was sure, would teach the same lesson.

His images were of rootless things. Papyrus cannot grow without a marsh, nor reeds without water; cut off, the godless man's hope dries up, a confidence as fragile as a spider's web that gives way when he leans on it. God does not reject the blameless, Bildad concluded, nor strengthen evildoers. “He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy.” It was a promise of restoration on the condition Job kept saying he could not meet: first be guilty, then repent, then receive.

Job granted the theology and attacked the courtroom. “Yes, I know that it is so, but how can a mortal be righteous before God?” If a man wished to contend with God, he could not answer Him one time out of a thousand. God is wise in heart and mighty in strength; He moves mountains without their knowledge and overturns them in anger, shakes the earth from its place, commands the sun not to shine and seals off the stars. “He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea.” He is the Maker of the Bear and Orion, of the Pleiades and the constellations of the south. “He does great things beyond searching out, and wonders without number.”

And that greatness was exactly the problem. Were God to pass by, Job would not see Him; if He took something away, who could stop Him, and who dares ask, “What are You doing?” Even if Job were right, he could not answer; he could only beg his Judge for mercy. If it is a matter of justice, who can summon God to court? His own mouth would condemn him. What Job wanted, and said plainly did not exist, was a go-between: “Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both.” Remove the rod and the terror, he said, and then I would speak without fear. As it was, he was on his own.

title: I Loathe My Life
subtitle: Job 10:1–11:20
description: Job loathes his life and begs for the charge sheet; Zophar answers that God could demand more.
paragraphs: Job's next speech opens with exhaustion: “I loathe my own life; I will express my complaint and speak in the bitterness of my soul.” His demand of God was narrowed to one thing, the charge sheet. “I will say to God: Do not condemn me! Let me know why You prosecute me.” Does it please You to oppress me, he asked, to reject the work of Your hands while favoring the schemes of the wicked? Do You have eyes of flesh, that You must search out sin like a man, though You know that I am not guilty and there is no deliverance from Your hand?

He turned to the making of himself. “Your hands shaped me and altogether formed me. Would You now turn and destroy me?” God had poured him out like milk and curdled him like cheese, clothed him with skin and flesh, knit him together with bones and sinews, granted him life and loving devotion, and preserved his spirit by His care. And yet, Job said, You concealed a purpose in Your heart all along: if I sinned, You would take note and not acquit me. The craftsmanship and the prosecution did not fit together in his mind, and he said so to God's face.

So he asked to have been unmade at the start. “Why then did You bring me from the womb? Oh, that I had died, and no eye had seen me!” Would God not withdraw from him a little, so he could have some comfort before going, never to return, “to a land of darkness and gloom, to a land of utter darkness, of deep shadow and disorder, where even the light is like darkness.” It is one of the bleakest prayers in the book, and it is a prayer: Job is still talking to God, even when what he asks for is to be left alone.

Zophar the Naamathite, the third friend, had heard enough. “Should this stream of words go unanswered and such a speaker be vindicated? Should your babbling put others to silence?” Job had claimed purity; Zophar wished God would speak and open His lips against him, and disclose the secrets of wisdom, for Job should know that God exacts from him less than his iniquity deserves. The heights of God were beyond Job's reach: “Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty?” They are higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol.

Zophar's prescription matched the others', with his own edge. Direct your heart, lift up your hands, put away the iniquity in your hand, and then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will forget your misery like waters gone by; your life will be brighter than noonday. But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and escape will elude them. All three friends had now spoken, in three different tempers, and the counsel had not moved an inch: Eliphaz gentle, Bildad blunt, Zophar sharp, all of them certain the diagnosis was settled and the cure was confession of a sin Job could not name.

title: Though He Slay Me
subtitle: Job 12:1–14:22
description: Job declares he will hope in God though He slay him, and wonders if a man will live again.
paragraphs: Job answered the three of them with open sarcasm: “Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!” He was not inferior to them, he said, and their proverbs were common knowledge. He had become a laughingstock to his friends, he who called on God and He answered. Yet he matched their doctrine of God's power and raised it: ask the animals, and they will instruct you; which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this? “Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His.” What He tears down cannot be rebuilt. He leads counselors away barefoot, makes fools of judges, loosens the bonds of kings, pours contempt on nobles, and makes nations great and destroys them. The friends spoke of a tidy God. Job's God reversed everything He touched, including, at the moment, Job.

In chapter 13 he stopped debating them and named his real desire: “Yet I desire to speak to the Almighty and argue my case before God.” The friends were dismissed in one line: “You, however, smear with lies; you are all worthless physicians.” If only they would remain silent; that would be their wisdom. Would they speak wickedly on God's behalf, show Him partiality, argue His defense without being asked? His majesty should terrify them out of it.

Then he stated his terms for the hearing, and at the center of them sits the most quoted sentence Job ever speaks: “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him. I will still defend my ways to His face.” He had prepared his case, he said, and he knew he would be vindicated. Only two things he asked: withdraw Your hand from me, and do not let Your terror frighten me. Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and You reply. And the question under everything: “How many are my iniquities and sins? Reveal to me my transgression and sin.” Why do You hide Your face and consider me Your enemy? Would You frighten a windblown leaf and chase dry chaff?

Chapter 14 turns from the courtroom to the brevity of life. “Man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble. Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure.” A tree has more hope than a man: cut down, it sprouts again, and at the scent of water it buds. “But a man dies and is laid low; he breathes his last, and where is he?” So a man lies down and does not rise, until the heavens are no more.

Out of that hopelessness Job wished the most daring wish of the speech. If only God would hide him in Sheol and conceal him until His anger passed, appoint a time, and then remember him. “When a man dies, will he live again? All the days of my hard service I will wait, until my renewal comes.” You will call, and I will answer; You will desire the work of Your hands; my transgression would be sealed in a bag and my iniquity covered over. Then the wish gives way under him, as water wears away the stones and torrents wash away the soil, so God destroys a man's hope. His sons receive honor or are brought low, and he knows neither. “He feels only the pain of his own body and mourns only for himself.”

title: Eliphaz Returns, and Job's Witness in Heaven
subtitle: Job 15:1–17:16
description: Eliphaz repeats the doctrine harder, and Job claims a witness and an advocate in heaven.
paragraphs: The second round opened harder than the first. Eliphaz no longer began as a comforter. “Does a wise man answer with empty counsel or fill his belly with the hot east wind?” Job, he charged, undermined the fear of God and hindered meditation before Him; his own mouth condemned him. “Were you the first man ever born? Were you brought forth before the hills?” Do you listen in on the council of God, or limit wisdom to yourself? Both the gray-haired and the aged were on the friends' side, men much older than Job's father. And under the argument sat the same foundation stone: “What is man, that he should be pure, or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?” If even the heavens are not pure in God's eyes, no man gets to claim innocence.

Then Eliphaz delivered the tradition again, the fate of the wicked as the wise men handed it down: the wicked man writhes in pain all his days; sounds of terror fill his ears; in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him; he despairs of returning from darkness and is marked for the sword. He will not escape the darkness; the flame will wither his shoots. The company of the godless will be barren, and fire will consume the tents of bribery. Eliphaz never named Job inside the portrait. He did not have to. He had described terror, darkness, and a marked man while looking at one.

Job's answer began in weariness: “I have heard many things like these; miserable comforters are you all.” If he were in their place, he could heap words on them and shake his head, but he would encourage them with his mouth instead, and his consolation would bring relief. Whether he spoke or held back, the pain did not change. God had exhausted him and devastated his family; He had seized him by the neck and crushed him, set him up as a target, and His archers surrounded him, piercing without mercy. “I have sewn sackcloth over my skin; I have buried my horn in the dust.”

His face was red with weeping and deep shadows ringed his eyes, “yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure.” Out of that contradiction came an appeal past the friends and past the courtroom entirely: “O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest.” And then a claim that stands among the most startling in the book: “Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high.” His friends were his scoffers; his eyes poured out tears to God. “Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!”

Chapter 17 is Job at his lowest in the round. “My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished; the grave awaits me.” Mockers surrounded him. He had become a byword among the people, a man in whose face they spit; his whole body was but a shadow. If he looked for Sheol as his home and said to corruption, “You are my father,” and to the worm, “My mother,” where then was his hope? “Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?” The second round had not moved the friends toward Job, or Job toward surrender. It had only stripped both sides down further.

title: Bildad's Net and the Redeemer
subtitle: Job 18:1–19:29
description: Bildad describes the wicked man's trap, and Job answers with the Redeemer who lives.
paragraphs: Bildad's second speech is the doctrine at its coldest. “How long until you end these speeches? Show some sense, and then we can talk.” Why are we regarded as cattle in your sight? The earth will not be forsaken on Job's account, nor the rocks moved from their place. Then the trap imagery rolled out, verse after verse: the lamp of the wicked is extinguished, his stride is shortened, his own feet lead him into a net, a trap seizes his heel, a noose is hidden in the ground, terrors frighten him on every side. Calamity devours his skin; he is torn from his tent and marched off to the king of terrors; the memory of him perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land. “Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God.”

Job answered from inside the picture Bildad had drawn. “How long will you torment me and crush me with your words? Ten times now you have reproached me; you shamelessly mistreat me.” Even if he had gone astray, his error concerned him alone. If they wanted the truth of his condition, here it was: “then understand that it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me.” Bildad's net was real enough; Job simply named a different hunter. He cried out, “Violence!” and got no response. God had blocked his way, stripped his honor, removed the crown from his head, and torn him down on every side.

Then chapter 19 lays out the abandonment, relationship by relationship, and it is the loneliest passage in the book. God had removed his brothers from him; his acquaintances had abandoned him; his kinsmen had failed him and his friends forgotten him. His guests and maidservants counted him a stranger. He called his servant, and the man did not answer, though Job implored him with his own mouth. His breath was repulsive to his wife. Even little boys scorned him, and when he appeared, they derided him. “All my best friends despise me, and those I love have turned against me.” His skin and flesh clung to his bones; he had escaped by the skin of his teeth.

It is from the bottom of that list that the plea comes: “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity, for the hand of God has struck me.” Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh? And then the wish that his case outlive him: “I wish that my words were recorded and inscribed in a book, by an iron stylus on lead, or chiseled in stone forever.”

What follows the wish is the summit of the book's middle. “But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.” “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God. I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. How my heart yearns within me!” The man who said there was no mediator, whose witness was in heaven, whose cry must not be laid to rest, now named his hope in a single figure. He did not explain it. He planted it like the inscription he had just wished for, and the debate went on around it.

title: Zophar, and Why the Wicked Live On
subtitle: Job 20:1–21:34
description: Zophar says the wicked triumph briefly; Job asks why they live on, growing old and increasing in power.
paragraphs: Zophar's second speech is his last, and he delivered it as a man whose thoughts compelled him to answer. His theme was brevity. Since man was placed on the earth, “the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary.” Though a man's arrogance reached the heavens, he would perish forever, like his own dung; those who had seen him would ask, “Where is he?” He will fly away like a dream, never to be found. Evil might be sweet in his mouth, but in his stomach it would sour into the venom of cobras. He swallows wealth but vomits it out. Zophar even assigned the cause: he has oppressed and forsaken the poor; he has seized houses he did not build.

The speech closed with the portion formula the friends kept returning to. The possessions of the wicked man's house will be removed, flowing away on the day of God's wrath. “This is the wicked man’s portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him.” As before, Job's name was never in it. As before, it did not need to be. Zophar had described sudden ruin falling on a rich man and called it the rule of the world, in the presence of a rich man sitting in ashes who kept insisting the rule did not explain him.

Job asked for the one courtesy they had stopped giving: “Listen carefully to my words; let this be your consolation to me.” Bear with me, then mock afterward if you like. Is my complaint against a man? “Look at me and be appalled; put your hand over your mouth.” When I remember, terror takes hold of me, and what terrifies him is the evidence of his own eyes.

“Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” Their descendants are established around them. Their homes are safe from fear, and no rod of punishment from God is upon them. Their bulls breed without fail; their children send forth like a flock and skip about, singing to tambourine and lyre. “They spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace.” And these are not secret doubters; they say to God openly, “Leave us alone! For we have no desire to know Your ways.” Yet God does not apportion destruction to them in His anger. How often, Job demanded, is the lamp of the wicked actually put out?

His closing evidence was the graveyard. One man dies full of vigor, completely secure and at ease, his body well nourished. Another dies in the bitterness of his soul, having never tasted prosperity. “But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both.” Ask the travelers, he said; the evil man is spared from the day of calamity and carried to the grave while watch is kept over his tomb. “So how can you comfort me with empty words? For your answers remain full of falsehood.” The second round ended with the doctrine not merely unanswered but contradicted by the world as Job could see it, and the friends had one round left.

title: Eliphaz Names Sins, and Job Seeks God's Seat
subtitle: Job 22:1–24:25
description: Eliphaz names specific sins the book never shows, and Job longs to plead his case at God's seat.
paragraphs: Eliphaz opened the third round by changing tactics. The general doctrine had not moved Job, so the accusations became specific. First he cleared the ground: can a man be of use to God? Does it delight the Almighty that Job is righteous, or profit Him if Job's ways are blameless? Is it for your reverence that He rebukes you? “Is not your wickedness great? Are not your iniquities endless?”

Then Eliphaz named the sins, one after another, as if he had a list from somewhere. Job had needlessly demanded security from his brothers and deprived the naked of their clothing. “You gave no water to the weary and withheld food from the famished,” while the land belonged to a mighty man and a man of honor lived on it. “You sent widows away empty-handed, and the strength of the fatherless was crushed.” Therefore snares surrounded him and sudden peril terrified him. None of this is anything the book has shown. The narrative of Job's life, from his early-morning sacrifices to the testimony of his own conscience, contains none of it, and the speech supplies no witness but Eliphaz's certainty. The accusations are his words, and the telling leaves them in his mouth.

His close returned to the familiar door. Reconcile now and be at peace with Him, and good will come to you. If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored; consign your gold to the dust, and the Almighty Himself will be your gold. You will pray, and He will hear; your decisions will be carried out, and light will shine on your ways. It was the warmest offer Eliphaz made, and it rested entirely on the charges he had just invented being true.

Job's reply is one of his most famous speeches. “Even today my complaint is bitter. His hand is heavy despite my groaning.” If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat. “I would plead my case before Him and fill my mouth with arguments.” Would He contend with me in His great power? “No, He would certainly take note of me.” An upright man could reason with Him, and Job would be delivered forever from his Judge. But east, west, north, and south, God was not to be found. “Yet He knows the way I have taken; when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold.” His feet had followed God's tracks; he had treasured the words of God's mouth more than his daily bread. Still, God is unchangeable, and Job was terrified in His presence.

Chapter 24 turns the argument outward again. Why does the Almighty not reserve times for judgment? Men move boundary stones and pasture stolen flocks. They drive away the donkey of the fatherless and push the needy off the road; the poor spend the night naked, without covering against the cold, huddling against rocks in the mountain rain. From the city, men groan, and the souls of the wounded cry out, “yet God charges no one with wrongdoing.” The murderer rises at dark; the adulterer watches for twilight; and no verdict falls in the open. Job's problem was no longer only his own case. It was that the court he kept appealing to seemed, from where he sat, to be holding no sessions at all.

title: Bildad's Six Verses and the Search for Wisdom
subtitle: Job 25:1–28:28
description: Bildad's last speech is six verses; Job answers with a hymn and the great poem asking where wisdom can be found.
paragraphs: Bildad's third speech is six verses long, and then the friends' side of the debate simply runs out. “Dominion and awe belong to God; He establishes harmony in the heights of heaven.” Can His troops be numbered? “How then can a man be just before God? How can one born of woman be pure?” If even the moon does not shine and the stars are not pure in His sight, “how much less man, who is but a maggot, and the son of man, who is but a worm!” It was the doctrine one final time, reduced to its smallest form, and Zophar did not speak again at all. The third round has only two voices in it, and the second is Job's, at length.

Job received the six verses with withering courtesy. “How you have helped the powerless and saved the arm that is feeble! How you have counseled the unwise and provided fully sound insight!” Then he answered the theology with a hymn bigger than Bildad's. The dead tremble beneath the waters; Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering. “He stretches out the north over empty space; He hangs the earth upon nothing.” He wraps the waters in His clouds, covers the face of the moon, inscribes a horizon on the waters, and by His breath the skies were cleared. “Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways; how faint is the whisper we hear of Him! Who then can understand the thunder of His power?”

In chapter 27 Job continued his discourse and swore to his position. “As surely as God lives, who has deprived me of justice,” as long as breath is in him, his lips will not speak wickedness and his tongue will not utter deceit. “I will never say that you are right; I will maintain my integrity until I die.” He would cling to his righteousness and never let go, and his conscience did not accuse him. Then, to show he knew their sermon as well as they did, he delivered it himself: this is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage the ruthless receive, sons destined for the sword, silver heaped like dust for the righteous to divide, terrors like a flood. Job could preach the doctrine perfectly. What he denied was that it described him.

Then the discourse lifts into the book's great poem about wisdom. Men can find anything buried: there is a mine for silver, iron is taken from the earth, copper is smelted from ore. Man puts an end to the darkness, cuts shafts in places forgotten by the foot of man, overturns mountains at their base, and brings what is hidden to light. “But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell?” Not in the land of the living. The ocean depths say, “It is not in me.” It cannot be bought with the gold of Ophir, onyx, sapphire, or rubies. Abaddon and Death say only, “We have heard a rumor about it.”

“But God understands its way, and He knows its place.” When God fixed the weight of the wind, measured the waters, set a limit for the rain, and made a path for the thunderbolt, He looked at wisdom, appraised it, established it, and searched it out. And He said to man the one sentence of it given to human beings: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.” They are the book's own opening words about Job, fearing God and shunning evil, now spoken from inside his longest speech, by a man who still had no answer to his question and was holding on to the definition anyway.

title: The Signature: Job's Oath of Innocence
subtitle: Job 29:1–31:40
description: Job remembers the gate where he defended the poor, swears his oath of innocence charge by charge, and signs it.
paragraphs: Job's final speech begins in memory. “How I long for the months gone by, for the days when God watched over me,” when His lamp shone above Job's head and by His light he walked through darkness, when the friendship of God rested on his tent and his children were around him and his steps were bathed in cream. He remembered his seat at the city gate, where the young men saw him and withdrew, the old men rose to their feet, and the princes covered their mouths and kept silent, because of what he had done there: “because I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper.” The dying man blessed him, and he made the widow's heart sing for joy. “I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban.” He served as eyes to the blind and feet to the lame; he was a father to the needy and took up the case of the stranger; “I shattered the fangs of the unjust and snatched the prey from his teeth.”

Chapter 30 sets the present against that past, line by line. “But now they mock me, men younger than I am, whose fathers I would have refused to put with my sheep dogs.” He had become a byword among them; they did not hesitate to spit in his face. His soul was poured out within him, the night pierced his bones, and his gnawing pains never rested. “I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me.” He had wept for those in trouble and grieved for the needy, but when he hoped for good, evil came; when he looked for light, darkness fell. His harp was tuned to mourning and his flute to the sound of weeping.

Then, in chapter 31, Job swears his oath of innocence, charge by charge, calling down penalties on himself if any of it is false. “I have made a covenant with my eyes. How then could I gaze with desire at a virgin?” If he had walked in falsehood, let God weigh him with honest scales. If his heart had been enticed by his neighbor's wife, let his own wife grind grain for another. On his servants' rights he was explicit: if he had rejected the cause of his manservant or maidservant when they complained, what would he do when God rose to judge? “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?”

The oath reads, point for point, like an answer to Eliphaz's invented list. Denied the desires of the poor? From his youth he had reared the fatherless as a father. Eaten his morsel alone? No stranger had to lodge on the street, for his door was open to the traveler. Trusted in gold? Put his trust in it and he would have denied God on high. Rejoiced at an enemy's ruin? He had not allowed his mouth to sin by asking for his life with a curse. Lifted his hand against the fatherless because he had support in the gate? Then his own curse on himself: “then may my arm fall from my shoulder and be torn from its socket.”

He ended the oath by signing it. “Oh, that I had one to hear me! Here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me; let my accuser compose an indictment.” He would carry that indictment on his shoulder and wear it like a crown; he would give account of all his steps and approach God like a prince. If his land cried out against him and he had devoured its produce without payment, let briers grow instead of wheat. Then the narrator closes the long debate with a flat, final sentence: “Thus conclude the words of Job.” Job had filed his case. What he had asked for, three rounds in the asking, was a hearing.

title: Elihu Burns with Anger
subtitle: Job 32:1–34:37
description: A young man who has listened to the whole debate burns with anger at both sides and claims God speaks through suffering.
paragraphs: When Job finished, the three friends stopped answering him, because he was righteous in his own eyes. That is when a fourth voice, silent until now, caught fire. Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger against Job for justifying himself rather than God, and he burned with anger against the three friends because they had failed to refute Job, and yet had condemned him. He had waited out of respect for their age. Now that they had no reply left, his anger was kindled.

His opening was an apology for speaking at all. “I am young in years, while you are old; that is why I was timid and afraid to tell you what I know.” But age, he argued, is not where wisdom lives: “But there is a spirit in a man, the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding.” He had listened to the whole debate and found no winner in it: no one had proved Job wrong. “For I am full of words, and my spirit within me compels me.” Like unvented wine about to burst a new wineskin, he had to speak, and he promised to be partial to no one and flatter no man, since he did not know how to flatter and his Maker would remove him in an instant if he tried.

His first speech claimed the same ground Job stood on. “The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.” He too was formed from clay; Job need not fear him. Then he quoted Job's own words back at him, accurately: I am pure, without transgression, yet God finds occasions against me, counts me His enemy, puts my feet in the stocks. “Behold, you are not right in this matter. I will answer you, for God is greater than man.” Why do you complain that He answers nothing, Elihu asked, when God speaks in one way and in another and no one notices: in dreams and night visions He opens men's ears and terrifies them with warnings, to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride, and preserve his soul from the Pit.

Elihu described God chastening a man on his bed with pain until his flesh wastes away, and then the turn, in words that sound like an answer to Job's own wish for a mediator: “Yet if there is a messenger on his side, one mediator in a thousand, to tell a man what is right for him,” to be gracious and say the man is ransomed from the Pit, then his flesh is refreshed like a child's, he prays to God and finds favor, and he sings before men: “I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved.” All these things, Elihu said, God does to a man two or even three times, to bring back his soul from the Pit.

His second speech, aimed at the wise men listening, sharpened into verdict. He quoted Job again: “I am righteous, yet God has deprived me of justice.” What man is like Job, he demanded, who drinks up derision like water and keeps company with evildoers? “Far be it from God to do wrong, and from the Almighty to act unjustly.” God repays a man according to his deeds; His eyes are on the ways of a man and He sees his every step; there is no darkness where workers of iniquity can hide. Elihu's conclusion was total: “Job speaks without knowledge; his words lack insight.” Job had added rebellion to his sin, he said, and multiplied his words against God. The youngest man at the ash heap had now said, in his own way, what the old men had said before him, and claimed more certainty than any of them.

title: Elihu: God Is Great, Beyond Our Knowledge
subtitle: Job 35:1–37:24
description: Elihu finishes inside a rising storm, telling Job to stand still and consider the wonders of God.
paragraphs: Elihu's third speech took up Job's claim to be more righteous than God and the question Job had asked in his pain: what does it profit a man? Look to the heavens and see, Elihu said; gaze at the clouds high above you. If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him? If you are righteous, what do you give Him, or what does He receive from your hand? A man's wickedness and righteousness affect men like himself. People cry out under oppression, he admitted, but no one asks, “Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night,” and God does not listen to empty pleas. Your case is before Him, Elihu told Job. You must wait for Him.

The fourth speech began with a request for a little more patience, and a promise: “and I will show you that there is more to be said on God’s behalf.” “I get my knowledge from afar, and I will ascribe justice to my Maker.” God is mighty, Elihu declared, but He despises no one; He does not keep the wicked alive, but He grants justice to the afflicted, and He does not take His eyes off the righteous. This was Elihu's version of the old doctrine, rebuilt as teaching: if men are bound with chains and caught in cords of affliction, then God tells them their deeds and opens their ears to correction. If they obey, they end their days in prosperity. If not, they perish.

“God rescues the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ears in oppression.” That sentence is the heart of Elihu's whole case, the claim that suffering is a classroom and not only a courtroom. He turned it on Job directly: you are laden with the judgment due the wicked; do not let a bribe lead you astray; do not long for the night; be careful not to turn to iniquity, “for this you have preferred to affliction.” Then his eyes lifted off the argument altogether, toward the weather. “Behold, God is exalted in His power. Who is a teacher like Him?” He draws up drops of water that distill the rain from the mist; the clouds pour out and shower abundantly on mankind; the thunder declares His presence, and even the cattle regard the rising storm.

Chapter 37 is Elihu inside the storm he is describing. “At this my heart also pounds and leaps from its place.” Listen closely to the thunder of His voice: He unleashes His lightning beneath the whole sky, says to the snow, “Fall on the earth,” and by the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen. The clouds swirl about at His direction, accomplishing all that He commands over the face of the earth, “Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion.”

Then Elihu turned to the man in the ashes with the sentence that ends the human half of the book: “Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the wonders of God.” The Almighty is beyond our reach, exalted in power; in His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress, and He is not partial to the wise in heart. Elihu was the last man to speak. The storm he had been describing as a picture of God's voice was, by then, no longer only a picture. Something was about to speak out of it.

title: Where Were You? The LORD Answers
subtitle: Job 38:1–39:30
description: God answers out of the whirlwind, questioning Job about the foundations of the earth and the wild animals.
paragraphs: “Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:” The hearing Job had demanded for three rounds, signed for with his oath, arrived, but not as Job pictured it. God did not take the witness stand. He took the questioner's place. “Who is this who obscures My counsel by words without knowledge? Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me.”

The questions began at the beginning. “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding.” Who fixed its measurements, and who laid its cornerstone, “while the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?” Who enclosed the sea behind doors when it burst forth from the womb, made the clouds its garment, and said to its proud waves: “You may come this far, but no farther; here your proud waves must stop”? Have you commanded the morning in your days, or journeyed to the vents of the sea, or seen the gates of the shadow of death? There is no charge sheet anywhere in it, and no mention of Job's sins, his case, or his losses. The subject is the world, and Job's size inside it.

The survey ran on through the sky and the weather. Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or the storehouses of hail, held in reserve for the day of war and battle? Who cuts a channel for the flood and brings rain “on a barren land, on a desert where no man lives,” rain spent where no one needs it and no one sees it? Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loosen the belt of Orion, lead out the Bear and her cubs, or send the lightning bolts on their way? Who has put wisdom in the heart? The questions are not answered in the text. They are not the kind that take answers.

Then the cross-examination walked into the animal world, creature by creature. Can you hunt prey for the lioness? Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God? Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Who set the wild donkey free to roam the salt flats, scorning the tumult of the city? Will the wild ox consent to serve you, stay by your manger, plow your valleys? Can you trust him to gather your grain?

The last three animals read like a deliberate comedy of human helplessness. The ostrich leaves her eggs on the ground, forgets a foot may crush them, and treats her young harshly, “For God has deprived her of wisdom,” yet when she spreads her wings she laughs at the horse and its rider. And the horse: “Do you give strength to the horse or adorn his neck with a mane?” He paws in the valley, laughs at fear, does not turn back from the sword, and snorts with fervor at the blast of the horn. Does the hawk take flight by your understanding, or the eagle soar at your command, lodging on a rocky crag, where his young ones feast on blood? By the end of chapter 39, God had asked about the earth, the sea, the dawn, death, snow, rain, stars, lightning, lions, ravens, goats, donkeys, oxen, ostriches, horses, hawks, and eagles. He had not asked one question about the case. Job had wanted a hearing about himself. What he got was a tour of everything that was not himself, and it was not finished.

title: Behemoth and Leviathan
subtitle: Job 40:1–41:34
description: Job places his hand over his mouth, and God presents two creatures no man can master.
paragraphs: The LORD paused in His questioning: “Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty? Let him who argues with God give an answer.” Job's reply is four sentences long, and it is the sound of a man whose case has gone quiet in his own hands. “Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth.” He had spoken once, he said, but had no answer; twice, but he had nothing to add.

Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind a second time, and the second speech goes for the root of the whole complaint. “Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me. Would you really annul My justice? Would you condemn Me to justify yourself?” Do you have an arm like God's, or a voice that thunders like His? Then adorn yourself with majesty and splendor, unleash the fury of your wrath, look on every proud man and bring him low, trample the wicked where they stand. “Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you.” Job had argued that God's government of the world was unjust because of how it treated him. God's answer is to offer him the job of governing it, and let the offer speak for itself.

Then the speech turns to a single animal, described at the length of a field guide. “Look at Behemoth, which I made along with you. He feeds on grass like an ox.” The strength is in his loins and the power in the muscles of his belly; his tail sways like a cedar; his bones are tubes of bronze and his limbs are rods of iron. “He is the foremost of God’s works; only his Maker can draw the sword against him.” He lies under the lotus plants, hidden among the reeds of the marsh, the willows of the brook around him. Though the river rages, he is unafraid; he remains secure though the Jordan surges to his mouth. Can anyone capture him as he looks on, or pierce his nose with a snare? The text does not name what animal this is, and generations of readers have argued over it. What the text itself insists on is simpler: God made him, God describes him with pride, and no man can handle him.

The second creature takes the whole of chapter 41. “Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook or tie down his tongue with a rope?” Will he beg you for mercy or speak to you softly? Will he make a covenant to be your slave for life, or be kept as a pet on a leash for your maidens? Hope of overcoming him is false; the sight of him is overwhelming. Then the challenge underneath the whole portrait: “No one is so fierce as to rouse Leviathan. Then who is able to stand against Me? Who has given to Me that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is Mine.”

The description that follows is the most extravagant in the book. Leviathan's rows of scales are his pride, sealed so tightly that no air passes between them. His snorting flashes with light, his eyes are like the rays of dawn, firebrands stream from his mouth and smoke billows from his nostrils as from a boiling pot. His breath sets coals ablaze. He regards iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood; no arrow makes him flee; he makes the depths seethe like a cauldron and leaves a glistening wake behind him. “Nothing on earth is his equal,” and he looks down on all the haughty; he is king over all the proud. Like Behemoth, Leviathan is left unidentified by the text itself. He is simply presented: God's creature, unmasterable by man, and described by his Maker the way a maker describes the thing in his world he is least sorry he built. After Leviathan, there was nothing left to ask. It was Job's turn to speak.

title: Now My Eyes Have Seen You
subtitle: Job 42:1–17
description: Job has seen God, the friends are rebuked and forgiven through his prayer, and his latter days are blessed more than his first.
paragraphs: Job's last speech is six verses, and it answers God's questions by handing them back. “I know that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted.” You asked who it was that concealed Your counsel without knowledge; surely, Job says, that was me. “Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know.” You said, listen, I will question you and you shall inform Me. And then the sentence the whole book has been walking toward: “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.” “Therefore I despise myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.” Job had asked for a hearing, a charge sheet, a verdict. What he received was a sight of God, and in his own words it was enough to end the case he had spent thirty-five chapters building.

Then God gave a verdict after all, and it landed on the comforters. After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite: “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has.” The men who had defended God's justice with tidy doctrine were told their speaking about God was wrong, and the man who had accused God to His face was called, by God, the one who had spoken accurately. The remedy ran through Job: take seven bulls and seven rams, go to My servant Job, and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves; “Then My servant Job will pray for you, for I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly.” So Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar went and did as the LORD had told them, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer. Elihu, the fourth speaker, is not mentioned in any of it, neither rebuked nor praised; the text simply never speaks of him again.

“After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his prosperity and doubled his former possessions.” His brothers and sisters and all his prior acquaintances came and dined with him in his house; they consoled and comforted him over all the adversity the LORD had brought upon him, and each one gave him a piece of silver and a gold ring. So the LORD blessed Job's latter days more than his first: 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys, the livestock doubled to the head. And he also had seven sons and three daughters, the same number as before, the children new.

The daughters are the only children in the book who get names. The first he named Jemimah, the second Keziah, and the third Keren-happuch, and no women as beautiful as Job's daughters could be found in all the land; and their father granted them an inheritance among their brothers, a thing the text records without comment, in a book where almost everything else is argued over. After this, Job lived 140 years and saw his children and their children to the fourth generation. “And so Job died, old and full of years.”

One plain fact is left standing at the end of the book, and the telling names it once, here. Job is never told about the council in heaven. No one ever explains the hedge, the permission, or the two days his world ended. He asked for the reason through thirty-five chapters of argument, and the book closes without giving it to him, giving him instead a sight of the God he had only heard of, the prayers of his friends on his lips, and fields fuller than the ones he lost. The reader knows what Job never learned. Job died full of years without it, and the text lets that stand.
